claim: Cancer patients often experience changes in mental health.
source: Cancer patients often experience changes in mental health, prompting an exploration into whether nerves infiltrating tumors contribute to these alterations by impacting brain functions.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that is supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Tumor-infiltrating nerves connect to distinct brain areas in a mouse model for head and neck cancer.
source: Using a mouse model for head and neck cancer and neuronal tracing, we show that tumor-infiltrating nerves connect to distinct brain areas.
evidence: Supported by neuronal tracing experiments shown in Figure 1 and described in the Results section.

claim: Activation of tumor-brain neuronal circuitry altered behaviors including decreased nest-building, increased latency to eat a cookie, and reduced wheel running.
source: The activation of this neuronal circuitry altered behaviors (decreased nest-building, increased latency to eat a cookie, and reduced wheel running).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data presented in Figures 4, 5, and 6.

claim: Tumor-infiltrating nociceptor neurons exhibited heightened calcium activity.
source: Tumor-infiltrating nociceptor neurons exhibited heightened calcium activity and brain regions receiving these neural projections showed elevated Fos as well as increased calcium responses compared to non-tumor-bearing counterparts.
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data in Figure 2.

claim: Brain regions receiving neural projections from tumor-infiltrating nerves showed elevated Fos compared to non-tumor-bearing counterparts.
source: Tumor-infiltrating nociceptor neurons exhibited heightened calcium activity and brain regions receiving these neural projections showed elevated Fos as well as increased calcium responses compared to non-tumor-bearing counterparts.
evidence: Supported by Fos immunostaining data in Figure 3.

claim: Brain regions receiving neural projections from tumor-infiltrating nerves showed increased calcium responses compared to non-tumor-bearing counterparts.
source: Tumor-infiltrating nociceptor neurons exhibited heightened calcium activity and brain regions receiving these neural projections showed elevated Fos as well as increased calcium responses compared to non-tumor-bearing counterparts.
evidence: Supported by ex vivo calcium imaging of brain slices in Figure 3G-J.

claim: Genetic elimination of nociceptor neurons decreased brain Fos expression.
source: The genetic elimination of nociceptor neurons decreased brain Fos expression and mitigated the behavioral alterations induced by the presence of the tumor.
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 4B-D showing reduced Fos in TRPV1-Cre::Floxed-DTA mice.

claim: Genetic elimination of nociceptor neurons mitigated behavioral alterations induced by the presence of the tumor.
source: The genetic elimination of nociceptor neurons decreased brain Fos expression and mitigated the behavioral alterations induced by the presence of the tumor.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data in Figure 4E-F showing improved nesting and cookie test performance in TRPV1-Cre::Floxed-DTA mice.

claim: Analgesic treatment restored nesting behavior in tumor-bearing mice.
source: While analgesic treatment restored nesting and cookie test behaviors, it did not fully restore voluntary wheel running indicating that pain is not the exclusive driver of such behavioral shifts.
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 6C showing carprofen and buprenorphine restored nesting scores.

claim: Analgesic treatment restored cookie test behavior in tumor-bearing mice.
source: While analgesic treatment restored nesting and cookie test behaviors, it did not fully restore voluntary wheel running indicating that pain is not the exclusive driver of such behavioral shifts.
evidence: Supported by data showing analgesic effects on cookie test performance.

claim: Analgesic treatment did not fully restore voluntary wheel running in tumor-bearing mice.
source: While analgesic treatment restored nesting and cookie test behaviors, it did not fully restore voluntary wheel running indicating that pain is not the exclusive driver of such behavioral shifts.
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 6A-B showing partial restoration of wheel running with analgesics.

claim: Pain is not the exclusive driver of behavioral shifts in tumor-bearing mice.
source: While analgesic treatment restored nesting and cookie test behaviors, it did not fully restore voluntary wheel running indicating that pain is not the exclusive driver of such behavioral shifts.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential effects of analgesics on different behaviors.

claim: The prevalence of mental health disorders in cancer patients is significantly greater than in the general population.
source: The prevalence of mental health disorders (e.g. depression, anxiety, suicide) in cancer patients is significantly greater than in the general population (Carreira et al., 2018; Pitman et al., 2018; Walker et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: A cancer diagnosis increases the risk of mental health decline in patients with no prior psychiatric history.
source: For those patients with no prior psychiatric history, a cancer diagnosis increases the risk of mental health decline (Zhu et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Decade-long cancer survivors maintain an increased incidence of depression (approximately 12%) compared to the population at large (3–5%).
source: For instance, decade-long cancer survivors maintain an increased incidence of depression (approximately 12%, depending on the cancer type) as compared to the population at large (3–5%; Steel et al., 2014; Götze et al., 2020; Kuba et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: TRPV1-expressing nociceptor neurons are present in head and neck squamous cell carcinomas.
source: We have demonstrated the presence of TRPV1-expressing nociceptor neurons in head and neck squamous cell carcinomas (HNSCC; Madeo et al., 2018), melanoma (Balood et al., 2022), cervical (Lucido et al., 2019), and ovarian cancers (Barr et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: TRPV1-expressing nociceptor neurons are present in melanoma.
source: We have demonstrated the presence of TRPV1-expressing nociceptor neurons in head and neck squamous cell carcinomas (HNSCC; Madeo et al., 2018), melanoma (Balood et al., 2022), cervical (Lucido et al., 2019), and ovarian cancers (Barr et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: TRPV1-expressing nociceptor neurons are present in cervical cancers.
source: We have demonstrated the presence of TRPV1-expressing nociceptor neurons in head and neck squamous cell carcinomas (HNSCC; Madeo et al., 2018), melanoma (Balood et al., 2022), cervical (Lucido et al., 2019), and ovarian cancers (Barr et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: TRPV1-expressing nociceptor neurons are present in ovarian cancers.
source: We have demonstrated the presence of TRPV1-expressing nociceptor neurons in head and neck squamous cell carcinomas (HNSCC; Madeo et al., 2018), melanoma (Balood et al., 2022), cervical (Lucido et al., 2019), and ovarian cancers (Barr et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Nerve recruitment to the tumor bed is an active process that involves the release of soluble factors, including neurotrophins.
source: Nerve recruitment to the tumor bed is an active process that involves the release of soluble factors, including neurotrophins (Renz et al., 2018; Hayakawa et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2014) and neuropeptides (Kasprzak and Adamek, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Nerve recruitment to the tumor bed involves the release of neuropeptides.
source: Nerve recruitment to the tumor bed is an active process that involves the release of soluble factors, including neurotrophins (Renz et al., 2018; Hayakawa et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2014) and neuropeptides (Kasprzak and Adamek, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Tumor-released small extracellular vesicles (sEVs) recruit loco-regional nerves to the tumor bed.
source: Tumor-released small extracellular vesicles (sEVs) also recruit loco-regional nerves to the tumor bed (Madeo et al., 2018; Silverman et al., 2021; Amit et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature including authors' previous work.

claim: Tau, a neuronal marker, is expressed in MOC2-7 tumors as early as day four post-tumor implantation.
source: Western blot analysis of whole tumor lysate indicated expression of Tau, a neuronal marker (Georgieff et al., 1993), as early as day four post-tumor implantation, which increased over time (Figure 1A, Figure 1—source data 1, Figure 1—source data 2, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1A and quantified in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Tau expression in MOC2-7 tumors increased over time from day 4 to day 20 post-implantation.
source: Western blot analysis of whole tumor lysate indicated expression of Tau, a neuronal marker (Georgieff et al., 1993), as early as day four post-tumor implantation, which increased over time (Figure 1A, Figure 1—source data 1, Figure 1—source data 2, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by western blot data and densitometric quantification in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Doublecortin (DCX) expression increased in MOC2-7 tumors over time.
source: A similar increase in the neuronal marker doublecortin (DCX) was noted (Figure 1B, Figure 1—source data 3, Figure 1—source data 4, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1B and quantified in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: DCX is expressed in adult peripheral neurons, including dorsal root ganglia.
source: While DCX is well-known for its expression in immature neurons, it is also expressed in adult peripheral neurons, including dorsal root ganglia (Dellarole and Grilli, 2008), and in non-neuronal tissues (Bernreuther et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The DCX signal in tumors did not originate from MOC2-7 cells.
source: The DCX signal did not originate from the tumors, as MOC2-7 cell lysate was negative for this protein (Figure 1B, Figure 1—source data 3, Figure 1—source data 4).
evidence: Supported by western blot data showing MOC2-7 cells are DCX negative in Figure 1B.

claim: Immunohistochemical staining demonstrated the increasing presence of nerves in MOC2-7 tumors beginning on day 4 post-tumor implantation.
source: Consistent with this, immunohistochemical staining of these tumors with the neuronal marker β-III tubulin (β3T), demonstrated the increasing presence of nerves beginning on day 4 post-tumor implantation (Figure 1C–E).
evidence: Supported by IHC images in Figure 1C-E showing β-III tubulin staining.

claim: WGA tracer injected into MOC2-7 tumors labels neurites within the tumor.
source: Representative en face confocal image of WGA positive (red) neurites within tumor (F) and the ipsilateral trigeminal ganglion (G) from a mouse orthotopically implanted with a MOC2-7 tumor and intra-tumorally injected with the tracer.
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy images in Figure 1F.

claim: WGA tracer injected into MOC2-7 tumors labels neurons in the ipsilateral trigeminal ganglion.
source: Representative en face confocal image of WGA positive (red) neurites within tumor (F) and the ipsilateral trigeminal ganglion (G) from a mouse orthotopically implanted with a MOC2-7 tumor and intra-tumorally injected with the tracer.
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy images in Figure 1G.

claim: WGA positive neurons are found only in the ipsilateral TGM, not the contralateral TGM.
source: (H) Low-magnification section of ipsilateral and contralateral TGM ganglia from a MOC2-7 tumor-bearing mouse that was intra-tumorally injected with WGA. The V3 branch of the TGM is marked with an arrow. WGA (red) positive neurons found only in the ipsilateral TGM.
evidence: Supported by microscopy images in Figure 1H showing WGA labeling only in ipsilateral TGM.

claim: WGA tracer localizes strictly within the tumor and does not leak out.
source: (I) Compressed Z-stack of confocal images demonstrating restricted WGA (red) within the tumor bed (cytokeratin, green). Vertical and horizontal cross-sections highlight that WGA (red) localizes strictly within the tumor (green) and does not leak out.
evidence: Supported by confocal Z-stack images in Figure 1I showing restricted WGA localization.

claim: WGA injection into MOC2-7 tumors labels neurons in the spinal nucleus of the trigeminal (SpVc).
source: Examination of brains from MOC2-7 tumor-bearing animals revealed tracer+ neurons in specific regions including spinal nucleus of the trigeminal (SpVc), parabrachial nucleus (PBN), and central amygdala (CeA; Figure 1J). Sections of brain from these regions show the presence of tracer-positive neurons (Figure 1K).
evidence: Supported by confocal images in Figure 1K showing WGA-labeled neurons in SpVc.

claim: WGA injection into MOC2-7 tumors labels neurons in the parabrachial nucleus (PBN).
source: Examination of brains from MOC2-7 tumor-bearing animals revealed tracer+ neurons in specific regions including spinal nucleus of the trigeminal (SpVc), parabrachial nucleus (PBN), and central amygdala (CeA; Figure 1J). Sections of brain from these regions show the presence of tracer-positive neurons (Figure 1K).
evidence: Supported by confocal images in Figure 1K showing WGA-labeled neurons in PBN.

claim: WGA injection into MOC2-7 tumors labels neurons in the central amygdala (CeA).
source: Examination of brains from MOC2-7 tumor-bearing animals revealed tracer+ neurons in specific regions including spinal nucleus of the trigeminal (SpVc), parabrachial nucleus (PBN), and central amygdala (CeA; Figure 1J). Sections of brain from these regions show the presence of tracer-positive neurons (Figure 1K).
evidence: Supported by confocal images in Figure 1K showing WGA-labeled neurons in CeA.

claim: A larger volume (10 μl) of tracer injected into non-tumor bearing mice resulted in tracer labeling of ipsilateral TGM neurons and brain.
source: A larger volume (10 μl) of tracer injected into non-tumor bearing mice resulted in tracer labeling of ipsilateral TGM neurons and brain (Figure 1L).
evidence: Supported by confocal images in Figure 1L showing WGA labeling in control mice with higher volume injection.

claim: The nerve density and distribution present in the tumor bed are higher than in control mice.
source: These control studies indicate that the nerve density and distribution present in the tumor bed are higher than in control mice, with the consequence that a small volume (2 μl instead of 10 µl) of tracer is sufficient to result in nerve labeling.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that 2 μl of tracer labels nerves in tumor-bearing mice but not in control mice.

claim: The mapped circuit encompasses pre-existing connections to brain areas that regulate pain and affect.
source: The mapped circuit encompasses pre-existing connections to brain areas that regulate pain and affect (Yeh et al., 2018; Hu, 2016; Zhu et al., 2022; Russo and Nestler, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature on brain regions regulating pain and affect.

claim: Ipsilateral TGM neurons from tumor-bearing animals harbored increased expression (>fourfold) in genes involved in neuronal signaling/receptors (Gabrg1, Gabra4, Grin2c, Grm3) compared to control TGM neurons.
source: Compared to control TGM (non-tumoral) neurons, ipsilateral TGM neurons from tumor-bearing animals harbored increased expression (>fourfold) in genes involved in neuronal signaling/receptors (Gabrg1, Gabra4, Grin2c, Grm3) and synaptic transmission (Gria2; Figure 2A; Supplementary file 1; Michetti et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by qPCR array data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Ipsilateral TGM neurons from tumor-bearing animals harbored increased expression in genes involved in synaptic transmission (Gria2).
source: Compared to control TGM (non-tumoral) neurons, ipsilateral TGM neurons from tumor-bearing animals harbored increased expression (>fourfold) in genes involved in neuronal signaling/receptors (Gabrg1, Gabra4, Grin2c, Grm3) and synaptic transmission (Gria2; Figure 2A; Supplementary file 1; Michetti et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by qPCR array data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Fus expression increases within DRG neurons following nerve injury and contributes to injury-induced pain.
source: The gene demonstrating the highest increase in expression, Fus, was of particular interest; it increases in expression within DRG neurons following nerve injury and contributes to injury-induced pain (Han et al., 2023; Du et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Significantly elevated expression of Fus by ipsilateral TGM neurons from tumor-bearing animals suggests the presence of neuronal injury induced by the malignancy.
source: Thus, significantly elevated expression of Fus by ipsilateral TGM neurons from tumor-bearing animals suggests the presence of neuronal injury induced by the malignancy.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known role of Fus in nerve injury and its elevated expression in tumor-bearing animals.

claim: Tracer+ tumor-infiltrating ipsilateral TGM neurons show increased responsiveness to capsaicin compared to tracer negative contralateral neurons.
source: We found that tracer+ tumor-infiltrating ipsilateral TGM neurons show increased responsiveness to capsaicin compared to tracer negative contralateral neurons (amplitude, Figure 2B–D; the area under the curve, Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2B-E.

claim: Non-tumor-bearing TGM neurons elicited a normal response to capsaicin similar to contralateral TGM neurons.
source: Similar to contralateral TGM neurons, non-tumor-bearing TGM neurons elicited a normal response to capsaicin (Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: TGM ganglia from tumor-bearing animals show overexpression of the sigma 1 receptor (σ1R).
source: We tested whether this was the case using western blotting and discovered an overexpression of the sigma 1 receptor (σ1R) and increased TRPV1 phosphorylation in the TGM ganglia from tumor-bearing animals (Figure 2G, Figure 2—source data 1, Figure 2—source data 2, Figure 2—source data 3, Figure 2H and I).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2G and quantified in Figure 2I.

claim: TGM ganglia from tumor-bearing animals show increased TRPV1 phosphorylation.
source: We tested whether this was the case using western blotting and discovered an overexpression of the sigma 1 receptor (σ1R) and increased TRPV1 phosphorylation in the TGM ganglia from tumor-bearing animals (Figure 2G, Figure 2—source data 1, Figure 2—source data 2, Figure 2—source data 3, Figure 2H and I).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2G and quantified in Figure 2H.

claim: The σ1R is an endoplasmic reticulum chaperone protein that directly interacts with TRPV1 and regulates its membrane expression.
source: Of note, the σ1R is an endoplasmic reticulum chaperone protein that directly interacts with TRPV1 and regulates its membrane expression (Ortíz-Rentería et al., 2018), while protein kinase C phosphorylation of serine 502 and 800 of TRPV1 reduces the receptor's activation threshold (Bhave et al., 2003; Numazaki et al., 2003; Numazaki et al., 2002; Bhave et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Protein kinase C phosphorylation of serine 502 and 800 of TRPV1 reduces the receptor's activation threshold.
source: Of note, the σ1R is an endoplasmic reticulum chaperone protein that directly interacts with TRPV1 and regulates its membrane expression (Ortíz-Rentería et al., 2018), while protein kinase C phosphorylation of serine 502 and 800 of TRPV1 reduces the receptor's activation threshold (Bhave et al., 2003; Numazaki et al., 2003; Numazaki et al., 2002; Bhave et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: HNSCC-infiltrating nerves have a unique transcriptome.
source: Taken together, our data indicate that HNSCC-infiltrating nerves have a unique transcriptome and a heightened sensitivity to noxious stimuli characterized by an increased TRPV1 expression and phosphorylation consistent with TRPV1 sensitization secondary to oral cancer (Scheff et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by qPCR array data in Figure 2A and cited literature.

claim: HNSCC-infiltrating nerves have heightened sensitivity to noxious stimuli characterized by increased TRPV1 expression and phosphorylation.
source: Taken together, our data indicate that HNSCC-infiltrating nerves have a unique transcriptome and a heightened sensitivity to noxious stimuli characterized by an increased TRPV1 expression and phosphorylation consistent with TRPV1 sensitization secondary to oral cancer (Scheff et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging and western blot data in Figure 2, and cited literature.

claim: ΔFosB expression was increased in several brain regions of tumor-bearing animals.
source: ΔFosB expression was increased in several brain regions of tumor-bearing animals, while cFos expression was also increased in the PBN (Figure 3A–F).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3A-F.

claim: cFos expression was increased in the PBN of tumor-bearing animals.
source: ΔFosB expression was increased in several brain regions of tumor-bearing animals, while cFos expression was also increased in the PBN (Figure 3A–F).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3B and E.

claim: Neurons in the PBN of tumor-bearing animals show significantly higher calcium responses to KCl stimulation compared to control animals.
source: While baseline fluorescence was similar between tumor-bearing and control animals, that recorded upon stimulation (KCl; 30 mM) was significantly higher in neurons of tumor-bearing animals (Figure 3G, H, I and J, Figure 3—figure supplements 1–3).
evidence: Supported by ex vivo calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3G-J.

claim: Absence of nociceptor neurons in tumor-bearing animals decreased cFos in the PBN.
source: The absence of nociceptor neurons in tumor-bearing animals, however, decreased cFos and ΔFosB in the PBN, and ΔFosB in the SpVc (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence quantification data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Absence of nociceptor neurons in tumor-bearing animals decreased ΔFosB in the PBN.
source: The absence of nociceptor neurons in tumor-bearing animals, however, decreased cFos and ΔFosB in the PBN, and ΔFosB in the SpVc (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence quantification data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Absence of nociceptor neurons in tumor-bearing animals decreased ΔFosB in the SpVc.
source: The absence of nociceptor neurons in tumor-bearing animals, however, decreased cFos and ΔFosB in the PBN, and ΔFosB in the SpVc (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence quantification data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Nociceptor-neuron-ablated mice showed increased nesting performance compared to intact mice.
source: Nociceptor-neuron-ablated mice showed increased nesting performance (Figure 4E) and decreased anhedonia (Figure 4F) compared to intact mice.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Nociceptor-neuron-ablated mice showed decreased anhedonia compared to intact mice.
source: Nociceptor-neuron-ablated mice showed increased nesting performance (Figure 4E) and decreased anhedonia (Figure 4F) compared to intact mice.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4F (cookie test).

claim: Nociceptor-neuron-ablated tumor-bearing mice had smaller tumor growth compared to intact tumor-bearing mice.
source: This was accompanied by smaller tumor growth (Figure 4G) and increased survival (Figure 4H).
evidence: Supported by tumor volume data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Nociceptor-neuron-ablated tumor-bearing mice had increased survival compared to intact tumor-bearing mice.
source: This was accompanied by smaller tumor growth (Figure 4G) and increased survival (Figure 4H).
evidence: Supported by Kaplan-Meier survival data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: Both C57BL/6 and nociceptor ablated mice showed similar body weight loss.
source: While both groups showed similar body weight loss (Figure 4I), nociceptor ablated animals show a transient (Wk 1, 4, 5) decrease in food disappearance (Figure 4J).
evidence: Supported by body weight data shown in Figure 4I.

claim: Nociceptor ablated animals show a transient decrease in food disappearance at weeks 1, 4, and 5.
source: While both groups showed similar body weight loss (Figure 4I), nociceptor ablated animals show a transient (Wk 1, 4, 5) decrease in food disappearance (Figure 4J).
evidence: Supported by food disappearance data shown in Figure 4J.

claim: RTX-treated mice had significantly slower decline in nesting scores compared to vehicle-treated mice.
source: Although all groups displayed similar nesting scores initially, the scores in vehicle-treated mice declined significantly faster compared to RTX-treated mice (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by nesting behavior data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Body weight decreased in all tumor-bearing mice, but the extent of weight loss was similar between vehicle and RTX-treated mice.
source: Body weight decreased in all tumor-bearing mice, but the extent of weight loss was similar between vehicle and RTX-treated mice (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by body weight data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Chemoablation of TRPV1 neurons post-development resulted in a decrease in tumor growth compared to controls.
source: Similar to the developmental ablation of TRPV1 neurons, their chemoablation post-development resulted in a similar decrease in tumor growth compared to controls (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by tumor volume data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Wheel running decreased as tumors progressed.
source: We found that wheel running decreased as tumors progressed, an effect partially alleviated by carprofen and buprenorphine (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: Supported by wheel running data shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: Carprofen partially alleviated the decrease in wheel running in tumor-bearing mice.
source: We found that wheel running decreased as tumors progressed, an effect partially alleviated by carprofen and buprenorphine (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: Supported by wheel running data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Buprenorphine partially alleviated the decrease in wheel running in tumor-bearing mice.
source: We found that wheel running decreased as tumors progressed, an effect partially alleviated by carprofen and buprenorphine (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: Supported by wheel running data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Carprofen and buprenorphine alleviated the decline in nesting behavior in tumor-bearing mice.
source: The nesting behavior (Figure 6C), body weight (Figure 6D), and food disappearance (Figure 6E) were also alleviated by the painkillers.
evidence: Supported by nesting behavior data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Carprofen and buprenorphine alleviated body weight loss in tumor-bearing mice.
source: The nesting behavior (Figure 6C), body weight (Figure 6D), and food disappearance (Figure 6E) were also alleviated by the painkillers.
evidence: Supported by body weight data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Carprofen and buprenorphine alleviated the decline in food disappearance in tumor-bearing mice.
source: The nesting behavior (Figure 6C), body weight (Figure 6D), and food disappearance (Figure 6E) were also alleviated by the painkillers.
evidence: Supported by food disappearance data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Neither carprofen nor buprenorphine impacted MOC2-7 tumor growth compared to vehicle-treated animals.
source: Neither carprofen nor buprenorphine impacted MOC2-7 tumor growth compared to vehicle-treated animals (Figure 6F), but buprenorphine increased tumor growth compared to carprofen-treated mice.
evidence: Supported by tumor volume data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Buprenorphine increased tumor growth compared to carprofen-treated mice.
source: Neither carprofen nor buprenorphine impacted MOC2-7 tumor growth compared to vehicle-treated animals (Figure 6F), but buprenorphine increased tumor growth compared to carprofen-treated mice.
evidence: Supported by tumor volume data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Nociceptor neurons infiltrating HNSCC connect to a pre-existing brain-projecting circuit that includes the trigeminal ganglia, the spinal nucleus of the trigeminal (SpVc), the parabrachial nucleus (PBN), and central amygdala (CeA).
source: Here, we found that nociceptor neurons infiltrating HNSCC connect to a pre-existing brain-projecting circuit (Navratilova et al., 2016; Mercer Lindsay et al., 2021) that includes the trigeminal ganglia, the spinal nucleus of the trigeminal (SpVc), as well as the parabrachial nucleus (PBN), and central amygdala (CeA) (Ito et al., 2021; Jaramillo et al., 2021; Ge et al., 2022; Torres-Rodriguez et al., 2024).
evidence: Supported by neuronal tracing data in Figure 1 and citations to published literature.

claim: This cancer-brain circuit connection occurs independently of pain.
source: This connection occurs independently of pain, and this cancer-brain circuit drives behavioral alterations in tumor-bearing mice.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that analgesics do not fully restore all behaviors, particularly wheel running.

claim: The cancer-brain circuit drives behavioral alterations in tumor-bearing mice.
source: This connection occurs independently of pain, and this cancer-brain circuit drives behavioral alterations in tumor-bearing mice.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data in Figures 4, 5, and 6 showing that nociceptor ablation and analgesics affect behavior.

claim: Elimination of TRPV1-expressing nociceptor neurons reduces tumor growth.
source: While the elimination of TRPV1-expressing nociceptor neurons reduces tumor growth and enhances survival rates, it also highlights a potential therapeutic target for mitigating depressive behaviors in cancer patients.
evidence: Supported by tumor growth data in Figures 4G and 5C.

claim: Elimination of TRPV1-expressing nociceptor neurons enhances survival rates.
source: While the elimination of TRPV1-expressing nociceptor neurons reduces tumor growth and enhances survival rates, it also highlights a potential therapeutic target for mitigating depressive behaviors in cancer patients.
evidence: Supported by survival data in Figure 4H.

claim: Elimination of TRPV1-expressing nociceptor neurons highlights a potential therapeutic target for mitigating depressive behaviors in cancer patients.
source: While the elimination of TRPV1-expressing nociceptor neurons reduces tumor growth and enhances survival rates, it also highlights a potential therapeutic target for mitigating depressive behaviors in cancer patients.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the observed behavioral improvements in nociceptor-ablated mice.

claim: Substance P, released by sensory neurons, drives malignant cell proliferation and migration in HNSCC.
source: We have previously demonstrated that head and neck squamous cell carcinoma is associated with innervation by sensory neurons and that substance P, one of the principal neuropeptides these fibers release, drives malignant cell proliferation and migration (Restaino et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Patients suffering from HNSCC often experience depressive disorders, which are poorly managed clinically.
source: Significantly, patients suffering from HNSCC often experience depressive disorders, which are poorly managed clinically (Chen et al., 2013a; Lazure et al., 2009; Elaldi et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: TRPV1 stimulation is sufficient to trigger the activation of the AP-1 transcription factor within neurons.
source: For instance, TRPV1 stimulation is sufficient to trigger the activation of the AP-1 transcription factor within neurons (Backes et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: TRPV1 activation could occur in response to low pH, which is prevalent within the tumor microenvironment.
source: Such TRPV1 activation could occur in response to low pH (Boedtkjer and Pedersen, 2020) or hypoxia (Pocock and Hobert, 2008; Pocock and Hobert, 2010; Stevenson et al., 2012), which are both prevalent within the tumor microenvironment.
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature on tumor microenvironment and TRPV1 activation.

claim: TRPV1 activation could occur in response to hypoxia, which is prevalent within the tumor microenvironment.
source: Such TRPV1 activation could occur in response to low pH (Boedtkjer and Pedersen, 2020) or hypoxia (Pocock and Hobert, 2008; Pocock and Hobert, 2010; Stevenson et al., 2012), which are both prevalent within the tumor microenvironment.
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature on tumor microenvironment and TRPV1 activation.

claim: Tumor-released sEVs, which transport microRNAs (miRNAs), induced sprouting of loco-regional nerves to the tumor bed.
source: Alternatively, we previously demonstrated that tumor-released sEVs, which transport microRNAs (miRNAs), induced sprouting of loco-regional nerves to the tumor bed (Madeo et al., 2018; Amit et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claim: sEV-transported miRNAs could modulate various neuronal transcription factors and drive transcriptomic changes in tumor-infiltrating neurons.
source: These sEV-transported miRNAs could also modulate various neuronal transcription factors and, in turn, drive the transcriptomic changes we observed in these neurons.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on known mechanisms of miRNA action.

claim: Trigeminal ganglia neurons are composed of ~80% of NaV1.8+ nociceptor neurons, with one-half being peptidergic (TRPV1+, TRPA1+) neurons.
source: Trigeminal ganglia neurons are composed of ~80% of NaV1.8+ nociceptor neurons, with one-half being peptidergic (TRPV1+, TRPA1+) neurons (Kobayashi et al., 2005; Mickle et al., 2015; Mishra et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: In the TRPV1-Cre::Floxed-DTA mouse, peptidergic neurons are eliminated, leaving intact ~50% of pain-sensing neurons.
source: In the TRPV1-Cre::Floxed-DTA mouse, these peptidergic neurons are eliminated, leaving intact ~50% of pain-sensing neurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known composition of trigeminal ganglia neurons and the specificity of the genetic ablation.

claim: The remaining presence of non-peptidergic, largely MrgD+, neurons might explain why nesting behavior in TRPV1-Cre::Floxed-DTA tumor-bearing animals is only partially restored.
source: The remaining presence of these non-peptidergic, largely MrgD+, neurons might explain why nesting behavior in TRPV1-Cre::Floxed-DTA tumor-bearing animals is only partially restored.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the partial restoration of nesting behavior.

claim: Inflammation contributes to pain in cancer.
source: Inflammation contributes to pain in cancer (Renna et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Treatment of tumor-bearing mice with analgesic drugs (carprofen, buprenorphine) resulted in complete restoration of nest building.
source: Consistent with this, treatment of tumor-bearing mice with analgesic drugs (carprofen, buprenorphine) resulted in complete restoration of nest building and performance in the cookie test.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data in Figure 6C.

claim: Treatment of tumor-bearing mice with analgesic drugs (carprofen, buprenorphine) resulted in complete restoration of performance in the cookie test.
source: Consistent with this, treatment of tumor-bearing mice with analgesic drugs (carprofen, buprenorphine) resulted in complete restoration of nest building and performance in the cookie test.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data showing improved cookie test performance with analgesics.

claim: The constraint imposed by the tumor on behavioral activities that require the use of the oral cavity is mainly due to pain and not to the physical interference of the tumor mass.
source: These data show that the constraint imposed by the tumor on behavioral activities that require the use of the oral cavity is mainly due to pain and not to the physical interference of the tumor mass with the pattern of oral activities that need to take place for mice to perform the corresponding behavior.
evidence: This is an inference based on the complete restoration of oral behaviors with analgesics.

claim: Analgesic drugs can partially mitigate the deficit in voluntary wheel running in tumor-bearing mice, but fail to restore this behavior fully.
source: Although analgesic drugs can partially mitigate this deficit, they fail to restore this behavior fully, despite their efficacy in completely restoring oral activity behaviors like nesting and the cookie test.
evidence: Supported by wheel running data in Figure 6A-B.

claim: Carprofen and buprenorphine decrease inflammation.
source: Moreover, given that carprofen and buprenorphine decrease inflammation (Shepherd and Mohapatra, 2018), their ability to restore normal nesting and cookie test behaviors (which require the use of the oral cavity where the tumor is located) suggests that inflammation at the tumor site contributed to the decline in these behaviors in vehicle-treated animals.
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Inflammation at the tumor site contributed to the decline in nesting and cookie test behaviors in vehicle-treated animals.
source: Moreover, given that carprofen and buprenorphine decrease inflammation (Shepherd and Mohapatra, 2018), their ability to restore normal nesting and cookie test behaviors (which require the use of the oral cavity where the tumor is located) suggests that inflammation at the tumor site contributed to the decline in these behaviors in vehicle-treated animals.
evidence: This is an inference based on the anti-inflammatory effects of the drugs and their ability to restore oral behaviors.

claim: Systemic inflammation alone cannot fully account for the decline in wheel running seen in vehicle-treated animals.
source: Since both drugs were given systemically and each only partially restored wheel running, it suggests that systemic inflammation alone cannot fully account for the decline in wheel running seen in vehicle-treated animals.
evidence: This is an inference based on the partial restoration of wheel running despite systemic anti-inflammatory treatment.

claim: The inflammation- and pain-independent component of behavioral decline is mediated via the transcriptional and functional alterations in the cancer-brain circuit.
source: We posit that the inflammation- and pain-independent component of this behavioral decline is mediated via the transcriptional and functional alterations in the cancer-brain circuit.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the incomplete restoration of behaviors with analgesics and the observed circuit alterations.

claim: Behavioral alterations in tumor-bearing mice could be attributed to depression.
source: These alterations could be attributed to depression (Walker et al., 2014) or represent a competition between the energy demands of the HNSCC malignant cells and the host's skeletal muscles (Grossberg et al., 2020; Thaker et al., 2006; Kim-Fuchs et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Behavioral alterations in tumor-bearing mice could represent a competition between the energy demands of the HNSCC malignant cells and the host's skeletal muscles.
source: These alterations could be attributed to depression (Walker et al., 2014) or represent a competition between the energy demands of the HNSCC malignant cells and the host's skeletal muscles (Grossberg et al., 2020; Thaker et al., 2006; Kim-Fuchs et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Release of the neuropeptide calcitonin gene related peptide (CGRP) induces immune suppression in melanoma.
source: In the context of melanoma, which is innervated by sensory nerves, we identified that release of the neuropeptide calcitonin gene related peptide (CGRP) induces immune suppression. This effect is mediated by CGRP binding to its receptor, RAMP1, which is expressed on CD8 +T cells (Balood et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: CGRP-mediated immune suppression is mediated by CGRP binding to its receptor, RAMP1, which is expressed on CD8+ T cells.
source: In the context of melanoma, which is innervated by sensory nerves, we identified that release of the neuropeptide calcitonin gene related peptide (CGRP) induces immune suppression. This effect is mediated by CGRP binding to its receptor, RAMP1, which is expressed on CD8 +T cells (Balood et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: A study utilizing a different syngeneic model of oral cancer found an immune suppressive role for CGRP.
source: A study utilizing a different syngeneic model of oral cancer similarly found an immune suppressive role for CGRP (McIlvried et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Neuro-immune interactions occur at the tumor bed.
source: These studies demonstrate that neuro-immune interactions occur at the tumor bed.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on cited studies showing CGRP-mediated immune suppression in tumors.

claim: Neuro-immune interactions within the peripheral malignancy may contribute to the behavioral alterations observed in tumor-bearing mice.
source: Our current findings indicating that tumor-infiltrating nerves connect to a circuit that includes regions within the brain suggest that neuro-immune interactions within the peripheral malignancy may contribute to the behavioral alterations we studied.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the observed circuit connections and known neuro-immune interactions.

claim: A higher prevalence of depression persists among long-term cancer survivors compared to individuals without a cancer history.
source: Yet, a higher prevalence of depression persists among long-term cancer survivors compared to individuals without a cancer history.
evidence: This is consistent with earlier statements in the introduction supported by citations.

claim: Long-term cancer survivors who have received treatment and show no evidence of disease continue to battle mental health issues.
source: Having received treatment and showing no evidence of disease, these survivors continue to battle mental health issues (Götze et al., 2020; Kuba et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Individuals with cancer can live with malignant growths for extended periods, often unaware of their existence due to asymptomatic or nonspecific symptoms.
source: The human experience with cancer is distinct from that of mouse models; individuals can live with malignant growths for extended periods, often unaware of their existence due to asymptomatic or nonspecific symptoms.
evidence: This is a general statement based on clinical knowledge of cancer progression.

claim: During the undiagnosed period, the tumor-brain circuit might induce irreversible changes in central neurons through activity-dependent transcriptional modifications.
source: During this undiagnosed period, the tumor-brain circuit might induce irreversible changes in central neurons through activity-dependent transcriptional modifications (Yap and Greenberg, 2018; Takayanagi-Kiya and Kiya, 2019).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by citations to published literature on neuronal plasticity.

claim: Transcriptional alterations in central neurons, anchored in neuronal plasticity, adaptation, and behavior, may become permanent even after the cancer is diagnosed and treated.
source: These alterations, anchored in neuronal plasticity, adaptation, and behavior, may become permanent even after the cancer is diagnosed and treated.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on known mechanisms of neuronal plasticity.

claim: Understanding the specific transcriptional alterations incurred by central neurons is vital to reverse entrenched brain changes.
source: Moving forward, to reverse these entrenched brain changes, understanding the specific transcriptional alterations incurred by central neurons is vital.
evidence: This is a forward-looking statement based on the study's findings.

claim: Head and neck cancer occurs in males three times more often than in females.
source: Head and neck cancer is predominantly a cancer in males; it occurs in males three times more often than in females (Gaeta et al., 2023), this disparity increases in certain parts of the world.
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Males that do not smoke and drink have a higher susceptibility for head and neck cancer than females.
source: While smoking cigarettes and drinking alcohol are risk factors for HPV negative head and neck squamous cell carcinoma, even males that do not smoke and drink are have a higher susceptibility for this cancer than females (Park et al., 2022; Dittberner et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Female patients with head and neck cancer, particularly oral cancer, report more pain than their male counterparts.
source: In fact, female patients with head and neck cancer, particularly oral cancer, report more pain than their male counterparts (Bianchini et al., 2019; Reyes-Gibby et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Differences in tumor innervation exist in males and females.
source: These findings suggest that differences in tumor innervation exist in males and females.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that female patients report more pain.

claim: MOC2-7 cells are HNSCC cancer cells derived from a CXCR3 null mouse on a C57BL/6 background.
source: MOC2-7 cells are HNSCC cancer cells derived from a CXCR3 null mouse on a C57BL/6 background (Judd et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Implantation of MOC2-7 cells in male mice results in dense innervation of tumors with nociceptor nerves.
source: Their implantation in male mice results in dense innervation of tumors with nociceptor nerves (Restaino et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: WGA is a lectin molecule that specifically binds to sialic acid residues present ubiquitously on neuronal membranes.
source: WGA is a lectin molecule that specifically binds to sialic acid residues present ubiquitously on neuronal membranes. It has been used extensively to map neuronal circuits centrally and in the periphery (Borges and Sidman, 1982; van der Want et al., 1997) and is a known transganglionic and transynaptic neuronal tracer (McNicholas and Michael, 2017; Dumas et al., 1979; Sillitoe, 2016) making it ideal for mapping neural circuits (Tabuchi et al., 2000; Levy et al., 2017; Itaya, 1987; Itaya et al., 1986; Carson and Mesulam, 1982).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature on WGA as a neuronal tracer.

claim: WGA is a known transganglionic and transynaptic neuronal tracer.
source: WGA is a lectin molecule that specifically binds to sialic acid residues present ubiquitously on neuronal membranes. It has been used extensively to map neuronal circuits centrally and in the periphery (Borges and Sidman, 1982; van der Want et al., 1997) and is a known transganglionic and transynaptic neuronal tracer (McNicholas and Michael, 2017; Dumas et al., 1979; Sillitoe, 2016) making it ideal for mapping neural circuits (Tabuchi et al., 2000; Levy et al., 2017; Itaya, 1987; Itaya et al., 1986; Carson and Mesulam, 1982).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature on WGA as a neuronal tracer.
